rationale: B wins because it is more honest about readiness: it says the split-stack angle is "Honestly weaker than the others" and warns not to pitch it without "a named product manager willing to speak." A has solid bones, but "Productboard, Aha!, and Jira's PM-facing workflows" turns missing competitive proof into a headline-ready claim. B still needs cleanup for "spent years refusing to enter," but its proof discipline would save a founder from sending the embarrassing version.
gaps_in_A: "every software company that successfully expands its addressable market deploys sales headcount and a demand-gen machine" is a sweeping market claim not in the update. Useful tension, sloppy proof.
"Productboard, Aha!, and Jira's PM-facing workflows" invents the competitive set from outside the supplied facts, then treats it as pitch-ready.
"tools that have long drawn complaints about bloat, slowness, and over-complexity" is an unsupported complaint history. That needs sourcing or it comes out.
"The interface-philosophy question will surface in design and PM community forums within days" invents a reaction signal. Hope is not a peg.
gaps_in_B: "Linear opens the product-management market it spent years refusing to enter" is not supported. The update says expansion beyond engineering, not years of refusal.
"category-creation" is the wrong label. This is category-boundary or competitive-positioning analysis, not a new category being created.
"Stakeholder views are, by definition, for people who open the tool weekly, not hourly" invents user behavior and frequency. Could be true, could be nonsense; the facts do not carry it.
"roadmaps and stakeholder views are bought by product leaders and often approved by someone above them" imports a procurement model that was not supplied. Keep it as a proof question, not a premise.
